[21:28] >> Sure. So I guess Lucy, it doesn't mean we start telling the story at the end, but what I
what I mean is storytellers are people who just think a little bit before they open their mouths.

anything is. It's just simple decision- making. And in order to make a good decision, you have to
sort of know what you're aiming at. My son Charlie today built me

we can make good decisions in

[22:29] getting there. So when I start say start with the end what I do is the first thing I say to

[27:38] question is from Nasier. How do you find a place to start the story where there isn't
anything opposite of, and in quotes, how often will this happen again? End quote. >> So, I would say
almost all the time there's an opposite. And if there isn't, you're probably telling an anecdote,
right? I think that sometimes what happens is we're either telling an anecdote not

[28:08] recognizing it for the story it could be or we're just telling an anecdote. Let me give you
an example. Last night I played a game called 321 with my kids actually two nights ago. Uh we were
at a dinner and we were waiting for our food. It's a game we play in storyworthy. It's a really
great game. It's about finding stories in your everyday life. But we were playing this game at the
table and my son Charlie told me this amazing story about being at the beach with my wife and his
former preschool teacher collecting dead crabs and then he is told by my wife, "You can't take the
dead crabs home. Don't be an idiot." He

[28:40] was about eight at the time. So he stuffs his pockets with dead crabs and sneaks them home
and puts them in his bedroom. And then about 5 days later, he noticed his bedroom is smelling and he
can't figure out why at first. And then it occurs to him, "Oh, it's the dead crabs." So, he has to
sneak the dead crabs out of the house and into the trash can before me or my wife find out. I had no
idea about this until the other night when he told me about it. He had kept that a secret from us
forever. And he told it really well, much better than what I just did. And it amounted to an
anecdote because it's just a thing that

[29:10] happened to him. There was no opposite at the beginning, right? But with kids and a lot of
times with adults, they sort of stay in the shallow end of the pool instead of going deep. So, I
said, "Charlie, that's a great anecdote. can we try to turn it into a story? And he said, "Well, how
would I turn it into a story?" And I proposed to him. I said, "Was this an example of you
discovering that mom is correct more often than you think?" And he said, "No, it's an example of me
how I tend not to believe people and I have to learn it for

[29:40] myself." And I went, "Aha, that's a story. That's a moment, right? That is a real moment of
transformation." My son discovers through the dead crab incident that listen, I'm just going to be
plagued in my life with having to like prove things for myself. I tend not to believe people when
they say things. And now that he knows the ending, he can find the opposite of that. I said, "What's
the opposite of you discovering you have to sort of learn things for yourself?" And he said, "Well,
I remember I used to hope that adults were right and now I don't trust them anymore and I have to
find it out for myself."

[30:10] So, he sort of found the beginning and the end in the opposition. The problem was he just
told the anecdote and didn't really question or probe himself for the meaning of the moment. That's
very common for teenagers and little kids and younger people. Less common for adults, but also
common for adults. So, what I would say is that if you don't feel like there's an opposite of the
final moment to begin with, you're probably just needing to probe that story a little more clearly
and find what that story really means. Once you figure out what that story means and how it changed
you

[30:40] in some way, you just have to find the place where you were not changed. and that tends to
be the beginning. Or you're telling a fantastic anecdote, which I often say is cotton candy, which
is delicious, but forgettable. Meaning, you can entertain the hell out of people with an anecdote,
but you can't really change hearts and minds with them. Doesn't mean they're bad. They're lovely. I
love a good anecdote, but uh sometimes an anecdote is all it is. I hope that helps. I should get
